body:
Why linguistic provinces became a major demand

Linguistic identity was an important political issue even before independence. People wanted administrative boundaries that reflected the language spoken by the majority in a region. They believed that government administration, education and public communication would become easier when people could interact with institutions in their own language.

The Indian National Congress had earlier reorganised its provincial committees along linguistic lines at its Nagpur Session in 1920. This was an organisational decision within the Congress, not the creation of constitutional States. Orissa was separated as a province on 1 April 1936 under British rule. This is important when distinguishing pre-independence linguistic provinces from the first linguistic State created after independence.

The Dhar Commission, 1948

After independence, demands for linguistic States increased. The President of the Constituent Assembly appointed the Linguistic Provinces Commission, commonly known as the Dhar Commission, in 1948. It was chaired by S.K. Dhar.

The Commission examined whether States should be reorganised primarily on linguistic lines. It did not support language as the sole or immediate basis for reorganisation. It gave importance to administrative convenience, economic considerations and national unity. Its report was submitted in December 1948.

The JVP Committee, 1948–49

After the Dhar Commission report, the Indian National Congress appointed another committee consisting of Jawaharlal Nehru, Vallabhbhai Patel and Pattabhi Sitaramayya. Its name, JVP Committee, was derived from their initials.

The JVP Committee submitted its report on 1 April 1949. It advised postponing general linguistic reorganisation because the country was facing serious problems following Partition and independence. It nevertheless recognised that a strong and specific regional demand, such as the demand for Andhra, could be considered separately, provided its proponents gave up their claim to Madras city.

Dhar Commission and JVP Committee

The Dhar Commission was appointed by the President of the Constituent Assembly and chaired by S.K. Dhar. The JVP Committee was a Congress committee consisting of Nehru, Patel and Pattabhi Sitaramayya. They were separate bodies.

The Andhra movement and Potti Sriramulu

Telugu-speaking people living in the Madras State demanded a separate State of Andhra. Their demand was based on the desire to have a separate administration for Telugu-speaking areas.

Potti Sriramulu began a fast unto death on 19 October 1952 in support of a separate Andhra State. He died on 15 December 1952. His death led to widespread protests and intensified the demand for a separate State.

The Government subsequently created the State of Andhra on 1 October 1953, separating the Telugu-speaking districts from Madras State. It was the first major State created primarily on a linguistic basis after India's independence.

Remember the distinction: Andhra State came into existence in 1953. Andhra Pradesh was formed later, on 1 November 1956, when the Telangana region of Hyderabad State was merged with Andhra State.

Prelims focus

  • Dhar Commission: 1948; chaired by S.K. Dhar.
  • JVP Committee: Nehru, Patel and Pattabhi Sitaramayya; report dated 1 April 1949.
  • Potti Sriramulu died on 15 December 1952.
  • Andhra State was formed on 1 October 1953.
  • Orissa became a separate province in 1936, before independence.
  • Trap: Andhra State (1953) and Andhra Pradesh (1956) are not the same territorial arrangement.

[Sources: NCERT, Politics in India Since Independence, Class XII, Chapter 1, Challenges of Nation Building, section Reorganisation of States; GCERT, Social Science, Standard 9, Chapter 7, Post-Independence India, pp. 47–50; States Reorganisation Commission Report, 1955, Introduction; Nehru Archive, JVP Committee Report on Linguistic Provinces, 1 April 1949; Andhra State Act, 1953; Odisha Government, history of the formation of Orissa Province. Consulted 22 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Public mobilisation for a separate Andhra State, 1952.

title: Linguistic Demands and the First Commissions

body:
The States Reorganisation Commission

The creation of Andhra State in 1953 encouraged demands for reorganising other parts of India. The Government of India appointed the States Reorganisation Commission (SRC) on 29 December 1953.

The Commission had 3 members:

  • Fazl Ali: Chairman.
  • K.M. Panikkar: Member.
  • H.N. Kunzru: Member.

The Commission submitted its report on 30 September 1955. It accepted that language and cultural homogeneity were important considerations in determining State boundaries. However, it rejected the idea that language should be the only criterion.

Its other important considerations included:

  • Preservation and strengthening of national unity and security.
  • Administrative convenience and effective governance.
  • Economic and financial viability of the proposed States.
  • National development planning and the welfare of the people.
  • Linguistic and cultural identity and the wishes of the people concerned.

The Commission's proposed arrangement contained 16 States and 3 centrally administered territories. Parliament and the Government did not accept every recommendation exactly as submitted.

The Telangana question in the Commission's report

The Commission examined the demand for combining Telugu-speaking Andhra with the Telangana region of Hyderabad State. It recorded concerns in Telangana relating to revenue, employment, education, water resources and regional development.

The Commission recommended that Telangana should initially remain a separate Hyderabad State. It proposed that a merger with Andhra could be considered after the general elections expected around 1961, if a two-thirds majority of the Hyderabad Legislature supported unification.

The Government instead merged Andhra State and the Telangana region of Hyderabad to form Andhra Pradesh on 1 November 1956, following a political agreement that included assurances for Telangana. The later Telangana movement raised concerns about regional safeguards and development, and Telangana eventually became a separate State on 2 June 2014.

Constitutional authority to reorganise States

The Constitution gives Parliament the authority to change the internal territorial arrangement of the Indian Union. Articles 2, 3 and 4 perform different functions.

ArticleSubjectConstitutional function
2Admission or establishment of new StatesParliament may admit new States into the Union or establish new States on terms and conditions it considers appropriate.
3Formation and alteration of existing StatesParliament may form new States, unite territories, increase or decrease State areas, alter boundaries or change State names.
4Consequential constitutional changesLaws under Articles 2 and 3 may amend the First and Fourth Schedules and include necessary supplemental, incidental and consequential provisions.

How Article 3 works

A Bill for a proposal under Article 3 can be introduced in either House of Parliament only on the recommendation of the President. If the proposal affects the area, boundaries or name of a State, the President must, before the Bill is introduced, refer it to the Legislature of that State for expressing its views within a specified period. The President may extend that period.

The State Legislature is consulted, but its consent is not constitutionally required. Its views are not binding on Parliament. The Supreme Court explained this distinction in Babulal Parate v. State of Bombay (1960). Parliament may proceed with the Bill even if the State Legislature disagrees or does not provide its views within the specified period.

The Bill must pass both Houses of Parliament through the ordinary legislative process, requiring a simple majority of members present and voting in each House. It then requires the President's assent to become law. A special majority under Article 368 is not required.

Article 4 and Article 368

A law made under Article 2 or Article 3 may make necessary changes to the First and Fourth Schedules and related provisions. Article 4 expressly provides that such a law is not treated as a constitutional amendment under Article 368. Therefore, ordinary legislative procedure is sufficient.

The States Reorganisation Act, 1956

Parliament enacted the States Reorganisation Act, 1956 (Act 37 of 1956). Its appointed day was 1 November 1956. The reorganisation produced 14 States and 6 Union Territories.

  • 14 States: Andhra Pradesh, Assam, Bihar, Bombay, Jammu and Kashmir, Kerala, Madhya Pradesh, Madras, Mysore, Orissa, Punjab, Rajasthan, Uttar Pradesh and West Bengal.
  • 6 Union Territories: Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Delhi, Himachal Pradesh, Manipur, Tripura, and Laccadive, Minicoy and Amindivi Islands.

Important territorial changes included the formation of Kerala from most of Travancore-Cochin and the Malabar region, along with Kasaragod taluk of South Kanara district, the expansion of Mysore with Kannada-speaking areas, the enlargement of Bombay to include Saurashtra and Kutch, and the merger of Telangana with Andhra State to form Andhra Pradesh. Punjab also absorbed the former PEPSU territory.

The Constitution (7th Amendment) Act, 1956 accompanied the reorganisation. It removed the earlier classification of States into Part A, Part B, Part C and Part D categories and established the constitutional distinction between States and Union Territories.

Prelims focus

  • States Reorganisation Commission appointed: 29 December 1953.
  • Chairman: Fazl Ali; members: K.M. Panikkar and H.N. Kunzru.
  • Report submitted: 30 September 1955.
  • SRC recommendation: 16 States and 3 centrally administered territories.
  • States Reorganisation Act, 1956: 14 States and 6 Union Territories, effective 1 November 1956.
  • Trap: State Legislature's views under Article 3 are not binding on Parliament; consent is not required.

[Sources: Constitution of India, Articles 2–4; Report of the States Reorganisation Commission, 1955, Introduction and Summary of Conclusions and Recommendations, pp. 254–261, and the section on Hyderabad; States Reorganisation Act, 1956 (Act 37 of 1956), sections 3–12 and First Schedule; Constitution (7th Amendment) Act, 1956; Supreme Court, Babulal Parate v. State of Bombay, 1960; NCERT, Politics in India Since Independence, Class XII, Chapter 1, Challenges of Nation Building. Consulted 22 November 2026.]

title: The States Reorganisation Commission and the 1956 Settlement

body:
The bilingual Bombay State after 1956

The States Reorganisation Act, 1956 did not create Gujarat and Maharashtra as separate States. Instead, it created an enlarged Bombay State containing both Gujarati-speaking and Marathi-speaking regions. The former States of Saurashtra and Kutch were also incorporated into the enlarged Bombay State.

This arrangement brought together two major linguistic regions within a single State. However, political demands for separate Gujarati-speaking and Marathi-speaking States continued to grow.

The Mahagujarat movement

The Mahagujarat movement demanded a separate State for Gujarati-speaking regions. Indulal Yagnik was one of its prominent leaders. He was an important public figure in Gujarat and founded Janta Parishad in 1956 in the wake of the Mahagujarat movement.

The movement sought recognition of Gujarati linguistic identity through a separate State. At the same time, the Samyukta Maharashtra movement demanded a separate Marathi-speaking Maharashtra, with Bombay city included in it.

These parallel movements placed increasing pressure on the bilingual Bombay State arrangement. The issue was no longer simply one of administrative convenience; it had become a major political demand involving regional identity and representation.

The Bombay Reorganisation Act, 1960

Parliament passed the Bombay Reorganisation Act, 1960 (Act 11 of 1960) to divide the bilingual Bombay State. The appointed day was 1 May 1960.

The Act created two separate States:

  • Gujarat: Formed from 17 districts of the former Bombay State and specified adjoining villages. Its territory included the former Saurashtra and Kutch regions.
  • Maharashtra: Formed from the Marathi-speaking territories, including Bombay city.

Thus, Gujarat became a separate State on 1 May 1960. This date is celebrated as Gujarat Foundation Day. Maharashtra also celebrates Maharashtra Day on the same date.

Gujarat and the 1956 reorganisation

The 1956 Act created an enlarged bilingual Bombay State. Gujarat was created separately only in 1960 under the Bombay Reorganisation Act, 1960.

Prelims focus

  • Mahagujarat movement: Demand for a separate Gujarati-speaking State.
  • Indulal Yagnik: Prominent leader of the Mahagujarat movement.
  • Janta Parishad was founded by Indulal Yagnik in 1956 in connection with the movement.
  • Bombay Reorganisation Act: 1960, Act 11 of 1960.
  • Gujarat and Maharashtra were formed on 1 May 1960.
  • Trap: Gujarat was not created by the States Reorganisation Act, 1956.

[Sources: GCERT, Social Science, Standard 9, Chapter 7, Post-Independence India, pp. 47–50; Report of the States Reorganisation Commission, 1955; Bombay Reorganisation Act, 1960 (Act 11 of 1960), sections 2–4; Census of India 2011, District Census Handbook, Kheda, Analytical Note, p. 112, biographical entry on Indulal Yagnik. Consulted 22 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Citizens gather peacefully in a traditional Ahmedabad square during the Mahagujarat movement in 1956.
pictures.caption: Public mobilisation during the Mahagujarat movement, 1956.

pictures.alt: The bilingual Bombay State faced parallel linguistic demands in 1956 and divided into Gujarat and Maharashtra on 1 May 1960.

title: Gujarat's Formation and the Mahagujarat Movement

body:
The map continued to change

The States Reorganisation Act, 1956 established an important framework, but it did not create India's final State map. Further demands emerged from linguistic identity, tribal and ethnic identity, regional development concerns, administrative convenience and political settlements.

Important developments after 1956

  1. 1963 – Nagaland: Nagaland became a State on 1 December 1963. The formation followed the Naga political movement and negotiations concerning Naga identity and political aspirations.
  2. 1966 – Punjab reorganisation: The Punjab Reorganisation Act, 1966 came into effect on 1 November 1966. Haryana was created from Punjab, Chandigarh became a Union Territory and certain hill areas were transferred to Himachal Pradesh. The Punjabi Suba movement was an important part of this reorganisation.
  3. 1971 – Himachal Pradesh: Himachal Pradesh became a full State on 25 January 1971 after previously being a Union Territory.
  4. 1972 – North-Eastern States: Meghalaya was formed from Assam, while Manipur and Tripura became full States on 21 January 1972. Mizoram and Arunachal Pradesh became Union Territories under the North-Eastern Areas (Reorganisation) Act, 1971.
  5. 1975 – Sikkim: Sikkim became the 22nd State of India on 16 May 1975 under the Constitution (36th Amendment) Act, 1975.
  6. 1987 – Mizoram and Arunachal Pradesh: Both became full States on 20 February 1987. Goa became a State on 30 May 1987, having earlier been part of the Union Territory of Goa, Daman and Diu.
  7. 2000 – Chhattisgarh: Chhattisgarh was formed from Madhya Pradesh on 1 November 2000. Regional development and administrative concerns were important reasons.
  8. 2000 – Uttarakhand: Uttaranchal was formed from Uttar Pradesh on 9 November 2000. The State was renamed Uttarakhand in 2007. The hill region's geographical and developmental concerns were important reasons for the demand.
  9. 2000 – Jharkhand: Jharkhand was formed from Bihar on 15 November 2000. Tribal identity, regional aspirations and concerns about development were important factors.
  10. 2014 – Telangana: Telangana was formed from Andhra Pradesh on 2 June 2014. It became India's 29th State at the time of its creation. The movement was associated with regional identity and concerns about development, employment and the implementation of earlier assurances.
  11. 2019 – Jammu and Kashmir reorganisation: The former State of Jammu and Kashmir was reorganised with effect from 31 October 2019 into two Union Territories: Jammu and Kashmir, with a legislature, and Ladakh, without a legislature.
  12. 2020 – Union Territory merger: Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu were merged into one Union Territory on 26 January 2020.

Present administrative status

At the content cutoff of 22 November 2026, India has 28 States and 8 Union Territories. The 8 Union Territories are:

  • Andaman and Nicobar Islands
  • Chandigarh
  • Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu
  • Delhi
  • Jammu and Kashmir
  • Ladakh
  • Lakshadweep
  • Puducherry

The change from 29 States to 28 followed the 2019 reorganisation of Jammu and Kashmir. The merger of Dadra and Nagar Haveli with Daman and Diu in 2020 reduced the number of Union Territories from 9 to 8.

Prelims focus

  • Nagaland: 1963; Haryana: 1966; Himachal Pradesh: 1971.
  • Meghalaya, Manipur and Tripura became States in 1972.
  • Sikkim became the 22nd State in 1975.
  • Chhattisgarh, Uttarakhand and Jharkhand were formed in 2000.
  • Telangana became India's 29th State on 2 June 2014.
  • Current status: 28 States and 8 Union Territories as of 22 November 2026.

[Sources: State of Nagaland Act, 1962; Punjab Reorganisation Act, 1966; Himachal Pradesh State Act, 1970; North-Eastern Areas (Reorganisation) Act, 1971; Constitution (36th Amendment) Act, 1975; State of Mizoram Act, 1986; State of Arunachal Pradesh Act, 1986; Goa, Daman and Diu Reorganisation Act, 1987; Madhya Pradesh Reorganisation Act, 2000; Uttar Pradesh Reorganisation Act, 2000; Bihar Reorganisation Act, 2000; Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act, 2014; Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019; Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu (Merger of Union Territories) Act, 2019; Ministry of Panchayati Raj, Annual Report 2025–26; Ministry of Home Affairs, Annual Report 2024–25, Union Territories section. Consulted 22 November 2026.]
